text: Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Make yourself believe the truth of my words,—that certain moments are torn from us, that some are gently removed, and that others glide beyond our reach.

text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.

text: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: The most disgraceful kind of loss, however, is that due to carelessness.
author: Seneca

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.

text: Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro.

text: You do not run hither and thither and distract yourself by changing your abode; for such restlessness is the sign of a disordered spirit.

text: When then we are impeded, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves—that is, our opinions.

text: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: But if you consider any man a friend whom you do not trust as you trust yourself, you are mightily mistaken and you do not sufficiently understand what true friendship means.

text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.

text: Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it thou art hindered from some other better work.

text: Keep on as you have begun, and make all possible haste, so that you may have longer enjoyment of an improved mind, one that is at peace with itself.

text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses.

text: Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.

text: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use.
author: Epictetus

text: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Without philosophy the mind is sickly, and the body, too, though it may be very powerful, is strong only as that of a madman or a lunatic is strong.

text: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish with respect to externals.
author: Epictetus

text: That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: You must persevere, must develop new strength by continuous study, until that which is only a good inclination becomes a good settled purpose.

text: He is the master of every man who has the power over the things which another person wishes or does not wish, the power to confer them on him or to take them away.

text: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live.

text: For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.

text: Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: You understand by this time that you must withdraw yourself from those showy and depraved pursuits; but you still wish to know how this may be accomplished.

text: You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer.
author: Epictetus

text: Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are those swelling waves stilled and quieted.

text: We have reached the heights if we know what it is that we find joy in and if we have not placed our happiness in the control of externals.

text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting.

text: Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I, to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come.

text: Above all, my dear Lucilius, make this your business: learn how to feel joy.

text: Let death and exile and every other thing which appears dreadful be daily before your eyes; but most of all death: and you will never think of anything mean nor will you desire anything extravagantly.

text: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: The man who is goaded ahead by hope of anything, though it be within reach, though it be easy of access, and though his ambitions have never played him false, is troubled and unsure of himself.

text: Let not these thoughts afflict you, I shall live unhonored and be nobody nowhere.
author: Epictetus

text: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!

text: Yes, I do not change my opinion: avoid the many, avoid the few, avoid even the individual.

text: As a mark is not set up for the purpose of missing the aim, so neither does the nature of evil exist in the world.

text: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time.

text: I confess that we all have an inborn affection for our body; I confess that we are entrusted with its guardianship.

text: In every act observe the things which come first, and those which follow it; and so proceed to the act.

text: Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it.

text: Immediately prescribe some character and some form to yourself, which you shall observe both when you are alone and when you meet with men.

text: Use thyself even unto those things that thou doest at first despair of.

text: Let us cease to desire that which we have been desiring.

text: If it be not fitting, do it not. If it be not true, speak it not.

text: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life.

text: How ridiculous and strange is he, that wonders at anything that happens in this life in the ordinary course of nature!

text: On no occasion call yourself a philosopher, and do not speak much among the uninstructed about theorems (philosophical rules, precepts); but do that which follows from them.
